full_text:
Interviewer:	Are you doing aeronautical engineering then?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	And, are you going on a placement or not?

Subject:	I'm not.

Interviewer:	OK, the reason I ask is because we are mainly interviewing placement students but we do want to interview a few non-placement students to find out why they're not doing the placement. But the gist of the whole project is we're interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines to find out why they decided to do engineering, what they expect to get out of it, what their career ambitions are – things like that, but ultimately the people that are going on placement, we're going to go back and interview them again, when they're on placement, to find out whether it meets up to their expectations and the ultimate aim really is to make a practical guidance document for the Engineering Councils so hopefully it will improve the situation for women in engineering. I'll start by asking you a few background questions and then we can move on to ask about the course so far and what you want to do long-term.

Subject:	OK

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did maths, physics and geology.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm, it was just a normal high school.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it wasn't an all girls' school or anything like that?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I used to work at a factory for aeroplane assembly, during my summer holidays and they restore Spitfire and Hurricane, sort of with 1950's techniques. Erm, like I said I do – I go there every time I (got/get?) a few weeks off to do a little bit more, but not in the mainstream industry.

Interviewer:	Yeah, that sounds really interesting. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	Er, no but my dad's a technology teacher and he's – he's now a computer technician.

Interviewer:	OK then, when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I think it probably started when I was a child. I was one of these kids that always had Meccano or Lego and I just found that I had a knack for maths and physics, so I thought engineering would be great to do. Also, I wanted to be an engineer, as a career, that's what I wanted to do.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that anything else has influenced you, like your family or with your dad probably being involved in like technology, or anything like that?

Subject:	Er, I think it's very much my dad's influence. Er because he used to take me to model car racing and model air – you know – plane - flying things from a very early age.

Interviewer:	OK did you have much careers advice when you were at school?

Subject:	Er, I think I can remember one interview, where I just told them what I wanted to do and everything but not, not really. They've more taken an idea along that they'd tell you how to get where you wanted to be.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what did they say about you wanting to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, they said that was really good. Erm, and they said – I said aeronauticals and they said you know a few other engineering areas to look into.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much career research?

Subject:	Erm, yes, I went through probably about 15 – like a keeping of a folder of everything that looked good and kept on checking things out till I decided what…

Interviewer:	It sounds very organised.

Subject:	It was. I was a strange child.

Interviewer:	What is it then, that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, maybe it's just – it's really interesting. I look at everything and I want to know how it works. Erm, and with engineering, well they teach you how it works. Erm, basically – it's the jobs you can get with engineering are very exciting and – well, the majority are – and you've got the teams and other people with the same ideas, you know.

Interviewer:	That's what appeals to you about doing aeronautical engineering, did you ever consider any other type of engineering?

Subject:	Er, I considered a few types but with aeronautical it's – I liked it because it was so broad, you learnt everything from you know, electrical to mechanical to you know say systems and programming. But then the case studies are all linked to aircraft which was where my main interest lay, in the end.

Interviewer:	OK, that sounds good. How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

Subject:	 [This university] – I – well one of my teachers went to [this university] and he used to sing its praises, as an engineer. And I came here for 2 day erm engineering look around of all the departments – weekend can't remember what it was called – and I loved the campus. And when I actually came that was about 2 years before I came to university but when I actually went round all the open days it just turned out that [this university] – you know, it was the best and I'd had the best experience here as well.

Interviewer:	Did you realise when you decided that you wanted to do engineering, that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I did yes but the thing is with the way I was brought up, going to like model shows and you know model flying, it was quite often I was the only girl in the building and at the thing. So it turned out – so most of my friends, at a younger age, were male anyway, so it didn't seem to ..

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged, or enabled, to take engineering?

Subject:	Er, very much so – definitely. I mean if they are interested in it, because you find that not many females are actually interested in engineering. I don't know whether it's how they're brought up or – actually they should be forced into it, but if they have a general interest.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women aren't given the opportunity to have an interest, because they don't even know what engineering is in the first place?

Subject:	Er, yeah. Very much. I think it would be nice, if at younger age you could go into girls and say look, you can do it, it's not just for lads. Erm, …

Interviewer:	Yeah, and sort of raise awareness.

Subject:	Yeah, but it's very much – I think it's done from when I was at the age of 3 – I got my first set of Lego or something and my – I think when you're having – a girl having a very close interest, you know, or a woman that knows about engineering going in at a very early – you know, formative years.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Ooh, erm, you've got to be able to think logically, that's quite key for engineering. Also, I've met quite a few engineers that don't have any people skills at all and engineers, with a good degree, is going to be a Manager, so I think very much understanding how people work and so learning a bit about management – it's all pretty much key to engineering as a graduate.

Interviewer:	Would describe any of those things as more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	I don't know. Being general – almost sexist – I think females very much have the good people – good people skills but maybe I don't know, maybe not as logical in the way think – it's more emotional – I don't know.

Interviewer:	OK, What do you think are the advantages or disadvantages of being a female engineer?

Subject:	There's loads of – I think there's loads of advantages because as you are maybe the only female – one of 3 or 4 females in a room of engineers, erm you'll very much get noticed. And if you've got a viewpoint you'll find that people – you know, the men especially, will listen to you erm rather than maybe another sort of identical male. Erm, some disadvantages – I don't know, I've not come across that many disadvantages other than maybe with the older generation they see you – females – we have to work harder to prove, yes you are just as intelligent as the person sitting next to you.

Interviewer:	Have you ever felt like you have to work harder – is that just what you imagine it to be like?

Subject:	Erm, in some situations. If you're going into a group that's already formed it's quite hard to say, look actually I do have an idea and it's better than yours or you know, it might help it. But no, when I worked at (?) Assemblies, they were lovely old gentlemen and they erm you know once I actually started talking, I had actually shown an interest, they were very accepting.

Interviewer:	OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, this year it has. The first year I was getting a little bit disillusioned because it's all sorts of maths and all basics and there's no aircraft in it erm but yeah, this year's really good, actually learning how to design an aircraft from scratch.

Interviewer:	What about the gender proportions – what are the gender proportions on your course?

Subject:	Er, there's 9 females out of 140 people on the course, I think. It's a bit low.

Interviewer:	OK. What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, I think that the best thing is that everyone's sort of gelled really well. When we did a end of term sort of 2 weeks after everyone else has gone home and building model aircrafts and all you know, just playing – that bit's really good fun. Erm the worst bit's – I think it's the thermodynamics – I went to a module and I passed it and everything but I just didn't understand what was going on.

Interviewer:	OK, did you get any help with that then?

Subject:	Yeah, we had – the lecturer was great on it – we just – we all just kind of missed the point.

Interviewer:	OK. Overall then, are you pleased that you did choose this course?

Subject:	Very pleased. I don't think I would have taken any other course – looking back.

Interviewer:	Yeah, that's really good. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Er yes, [name] took us for dynamics and vibrations.

Interviewer:	OK, have you noticed any differences in the style of teaching of the male and the female lecturers?

Subject:	Mm, I don't know I can only really base it on just on one lecturer, because originally we had another kind of female lecturer but it was for kind of business, and it was completely different module that we were taught anyway. I don't think so.

Interviewer:	OK would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, I don't know if I'd find it more encouraging. It – probably it would be nice to see, you know, more women in you know – people that are in engineering but I don't know.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the female lecturer treats you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, she did. I mean she's got quite an interesting personality. She's – I don't know she's kind of funny in a very dry way, whereas some of the other lecturers are – I don't know – not funny at all.

Interviewer:	OK, what about the male lecturers, do you think they treat the female students the same as the male students?

Subject:	Erm, yes, I think they do erm there's only been one case where we've kind of – he's more of a technician, but he kinds of pats you on head and sends you off but no, it's all been very fair,

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	I do yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Yes – male.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with having a male tutor – do you find him approachable?

Subject:	Yeah, he's a brilliant chap, he's really interesting – yeah.

Interviewer:	You wouldn't prefer to have a female tutor then?

Subject:	Erm, I don't mind really.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know really. Er, one of our – teaching lecturers, he's really nice and he's always interested in what you want to do and what you're going to do and sort of banters you back about – erm, 'cos I wanted to be a navigator – why is a navigator getting an engineering degree?

Interviewer:	OK have you had to do a lot of group work as part of your course?

Subject:	Er, yes, quite a bit.

Interviewer:	OK, do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Er, I do in most situation's – I mean there's a – I like everybody normally, but there's one or two people on my course that I always get put in a group with and erm, I sit there and I just grit my teeth a little bit.

Interviewer:	Well why is that?

Subject:	Erm, generally he's the best thing since sliced bread and everything he's – everything you've done he's done 10 times better. He doesn't really take in your viewpoint. But he does that with everybody, it's not just females.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think males are more likely to have that attitude than a female though?

Subject:	Erm, ooh that's a hard one, erm, hmm, you know with – females that do engineering, definitely men will have more of that attitude but the ones I've met so far seem to be very level headed and nice.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you deal with that situation then?

Subject:	Oh it's – it's fine really. You just – I just sit there and nod and whenever we sort of carry on our discussions and – I mean he has some good ideas, you've just got to sort of filter them.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the benefits of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, it's (?) – especially with engineering if you're – we just designed a frame to take a certain loading, and there's so many areas that you've got to cover and sort of like – the analysis of stresses, and what sort of (routes?) you're gonna use, you very much need more brains. So each person can focus on a different bit. And if you're focusing on something different, it's always good to get them to look at your bit and you look at their bit, because you very much get caught up in one area and forget about another area because of – well it's just so broad – you've got to learn everything – loads of things about this one item you're making.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will help you when you go into the industry – the fact that you've done so much group work as well?

Subject:	Yes, very much.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Er, yes, I think they do. I mean I've worked within teams which I've been the only female in, and I've worked in teams which have – you know – are usually (?) male or female. Erm, I think with erm – with a male group it's normally quite raucous, by itself, but a female group brings a – sort of a very civilising influence into it. I remember from being a child that there'd be you know, basically the cars and then all these chaps would normally be mouthing off, and then you'd put a sort of 12 year old girl in the situation, and you've never met such polite like people, in the world, hopefully. But yes, stabilising influence.

Interviewer:	OK, you've said you've worked with male groups and female groups. Do you have a preference or aren't you bothered?

Subject:	Erm, I'm not really bothered. I mean – because the people – anybody you're working with in a group is so different, you couldn't really compare them.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing a placement?

Subject:	Er, I did yes.

Interviewer:	How did you decide not to do the placement?

Subject:	Erm, well I'm doing the 4 years masters – er and I kind of thought maybe 5 years is too long. Erm, I mean if I could – I could have done a 3 year and had a year in industry and realised that's good to employers because I'd done the year in industry and had experience but then I thought well if I do the – I want – I'm gonna – touch wood – I'll end up doing the masters and maybe in a few years time become chartered (yeah). And if – you know if I've got to do this masters anyway, I might as well do it all in a row, while your brains in the right gear than do a placement year.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on a placement?

Subject:	Er, I was actually – I joined the RAF as a volunteer reserve

Interviewer:	Oh yeah, I think you said that in your email (sorry about that) That's OK. 

Subject:	And they're not really into – well they are this year but when I joined they weren't really into people doing gap years because you have to leave your squadron, and then sort of re-apply (absolutely) and I didn't really want to lose you know, the opportunities that I had. Erm, but this year they actually do – they are including a placement year, we sussed it about 2 months ago, so I probably could've done that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any particular advantages, or disadvantages of doing the gap year?

Subject:	Er, disadvantages, as I've said to you – maybe a year out of the flow of all of your course. That if you get more money – so you can afford to stay for that extra year, but the advantages are very much – well one of my friends has done a 3 year straight – erm mechanical engineering course and she's going on to get a job in the industry and the first sort of 5 places she applied to said, oh we're just using people with a year's experience. Erm, because again there's so many people now with erm a Bachelor's course and their experiences – they can – you know they can pick and choose their graduate training schemes. So I think if I was just doing a Bachelor's I'd be a bit worried about not doing a placement year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that you're doing a masters counteracts that a bit then, when you will be looking for a job?

Subject:	I hope so, yes. That's the plan.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the work experience that you've done and the fact that you are a RAF volunteer, do you think that'll help when you're looking for a job as well – that experience?

Subject:	Yes, that's another thing that I'm hoping because I've had so much management and leadership training and you know they've taken me all around the world, so I such be a bold enough person without the gap year.

Interviewer:	How long have you been an RAF volunteer for?

Subject:	Erm, it was a year last December – it seems much longer.

Interviewer:	What sorts of things does that involve then?

Subject:	Erm, oh every Tuesday we have a training night er and we learn all about current affairs er what the RAF is, the aircraft coming in. Every free day I go to RAF [place] and I'm learning to fly erm on the – an air flight training scheme, which when I complete, I'll be streamed and then I can go on from there if I decide to join the RAF as a pilot or a navigator. Erm, you get adventure training, which is practically free. I mean I went to Egypt for 10 days for £110 and we did a 15 hour diving course

Interviewer:	That sounds exciting.

Subject:	And also, I've been to Tanzania for 5 weeks, built an orphanage with an RAF team and then went on safari with (?) (wow) – brilliant. But you have 2 years kind of completely free and then you have to apply – I've just applied to the RAF for – for the 4 day Officer's selection board and I'm just awaiting the results to see.

Interviewer:	Is that for when you've finished Uni or..?

Subject:	No, it'll be a bursary scheme, so I wouldn't be allowed to do a gap year anyway, if I get the bursary.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so they'll sponsor you for like your last…

Subject:	Yeah. So I went for my pilot in engineering because I have really enjoyed the flying and I thought well if you never have – if you never apply, you never try and I don't know you'll never know.

Interviewer:	I had flying lessons for my 18th birthday. What do you think have been the best things and the worst things about the RAF experience and the other work experience that you've had?

Subject:	Er, I can't think of any bad things. Erm, it was good. Well the only thing I can say is when you're in the RAF, everything that you do is assessed, every time you talk to one of the staff they make a mental note and it all comes down to a final year report, but my report's all been good, so touch wood I've achieved what they want – you know what they think's good enough.

Interviewer:	Have you worked with many women while you've been in the RAF?

Subject:	Erm I think – er not really erm other than people that are sort of my age, erm or in the non-commissioned ranks there's a lot of females but in the sort of pilot course I've mainly been taught by pilots and there didn't seem to be hardly any female pilots. I only know of er – I know 1 navigator and 1 pilot that are actually just starting their first tours.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the main skills that you'll learn from both the work experiences, that you'll take into industry with you?

Subject:	Er, with doing work on – in 1950's – you kind of learn a bit of history of flight and you've always got – if you're talking to another engineer there'll always be – or anybody really, they will always be interested about that, so there's always something you know, or what sort of (?) you can tell them about this. So, just kind of a general interest, you can get that from it.

Subject:	Erm, with the RAF it takes all leadership erm and you learn so much about people because you're put in very stressful situations and told right, can you get these people to you know do this. And you panic for a bit but then you suddenly realise that actually everyone's – if everyone knows you really, you can tell them what to do, and they do it, and they help you with suggestions and in the end you become – you know, you do become part of a team.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the whole educational experience and the way you're taught, reflects what it's like in industry?

Subject:	Er, I don't know. I don't think - industry – I have this idea of industry that it'll be sort of all kind of suits and big Board meetings and things like that. Whereas going to university in your jeans and baggy T-shirts kind of thing and sitting in front of a Board. I think where my course is very lecture based, and because of funding it's not very hands on and the team work is kind of more informal. Erm, I don't think it's exactly what industry will be like.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think it should be geared more to prepare you for when you go into the industry?

Subject:	In a way, yes. I mean systems is very geared up. I mean they have come into university, in suits, every now and then to do their big Board meetings and things. But, from a student's point of view you kind of don't want that hassle if you see what I mean.

Interviewer:	OK, do you hope to work for the RAF when you finish your degree then?

Subject:	Yes it is. I'd love to. I mean on the Squadron, I'm a navigator, but unfortunately they're not taking any more on, they've got too many at the moment so unless I – if I don't get this bursary I'll go in direct entrants and apply navigator first, then engineer. Erm, but I think the – well, I hope the outcome from this – I've just applied for – erm will – either be a pilot bursary, which I'd be over the moon with. Erm, but I think more likely I'll be an engineer but er that's what I hope to – if I accept the bursary I'll have to do 16 years, but that's what I want really.

Interviewer:	Fantastic. How do you think that work will differ from being at university, in terms of what's expected of you?

Subject:	Erm, in the RAF it'll be completely different. Erm, I've followed around the Engineering Officer for a day when I was on a flight station and you're taught – you're taught a very broad course, here at university but the stuff he was doing was completely different again because he had erm he was a junior engineering officer and he'd got 5 aircraft, he was responsible for keeping up and running all the time. He's got 160 non-commissioned officers that he was in charge of and he was – I think he was 5 years older than I am. Erm, that's the level of responsibility. He spent quite a lot of time sifting paperwork, another lot of time in high level meetings trying to convince his senior officers that yes, they will have their aircraft and no this one is very broken – you're not having it. It's all people skills. He only once or twice had to use his engineering background to say you know, no, this is – it's not fit to fly. But the degree is there for when you sign your name on a bit of paper and if – you know – the worst happens, it's mainly for what's your job title in court type of thing. See what I mean? It's more of a compulsory requirement, to be an engineering officer.

Interviewer:	Do you mind that or would you prefer it if you were actually using more of your degree or…?

Subject:	Erm, a good – no, I think I would really enjoy the people management. But as you progress up the ladder you need to use your engineering degree more erm because you'll be looking at bringing new technologies, which is eventually what I'd like to do.

Interviewer:	Do you still get your chartership if you go to work in the RAF?

Subject:	Yes, you do.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the main skills that you will use from the degree, when you are working? Do you think it will then be more like relationship skills rather than the actual technical skills?

Subject:	Er, yes, I think it will be erm I've done a few business modules and I think that will come in – they will be important. But from the degree, it's compulsory to be an engineer that you have a – you know, a technical background so I will use it as in I have to have it and I just find it really interesting anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think the best and the worst things about working in the RAF?

Subject:	Er, the best things are it's not just a career its a lifestyle – you've got – you know, you have to see – they own you for 12 hours a day and if they want to fill those 12 hours then they get filled. Erm but the opportunities are unbelievable. I mean I've only been in a year and I've you know, seen so much erm there's – I think the benefits of joining the RAF far outweigh, you know the disadvantages, 'cos obviously you are a member of a fighting force and if it comes to war you're going to war – that's what they pay you for. Erm, but you know it's just…

Interviewer:	Is that the only disadvantage that you could say?

Subject:	Erm, there's also one – if I'm a pilot I won't be able to have children till I've you know, done quite a lot of service, because obviously they've spent quite a few million pounds training you – they don't want you to suddenly get pregnant and run off.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all or…?

Subject:	Not really because my mum had me when she was I think she was 30 – my brother when she was 34 and by the time I've done my 16 years or done say 14 years and then doing ground tour I'll be about that age anyway, so, you know, touch wood I'll be able to have kids.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there's anything that will stop you from achieving what you want in terms of your career? Or any difficulties that you might face?

Subject:	I don't think so – apart from failing my degree, that would just stop everything in its tracks, but I can't really see that. Other than, you know, the worst happening at home and having to go back in…

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far or would you do anything differently if you had to go through it all again?

Subject:	Erm, I'm happy so far. I'll – you know, I'll let you know in a few weeks if I'm very happy or if I'm going back to the drawing board.

Interviewer:	Have you considered any other options if you don't get into the RAF?

Subject:	Yes, er I – 1 applied 2 years ago and er I was a little bit too young. You know they said grow up a little bit come back. And I applied for [company] undergraduate scheme, as well – sort of joint venture between [company] and can't remember – some other, other companies and they actually said, yes, we'll give you sponsorship. But by the time they'd given me a letter of confirmation, I'd joined the er Squadron and I'd got you know 10 weeks of adventure training. I just couldn't pass it up to do 10 weeks of work placement. So I rejected that but they – I think very much I wouldn't have a problem getting back into that sort of area so er yeah I'll work for the highest bidder.

Interviewer:	What sort of things would you be looking for in a company if you don't go in the RAF? What sort of things would attract you to a company?

Subject:	Very much good promotional prospects – er it'd have to be a big successful company er because they're the only ones that have good promotional prospects. Basically I wanted – I want a very strong company because quite a few little ones have been going under recently because of – you've got all the problem of the aircraft industry – they're moving it all abroad.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the engineering industry?

Subject:	That's probably the hardest question you could ask an engineers. Erm, challenging, fun, interesting, corporation, integral.

Interviewer:	OK, would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know. I suppose you would because it is mainly full of men.

Interviewer:	Do you think that is what makes it masculine – the numbers of men rather than the type of work that you're doing?

Subject:	I would say yes, I think, because erm I don't know if it was full of women you'd say it was feminine because obviously the industry takes on the character of the people that are in it. Erm, I don't know – traditionally it's very masculine because you know boys play with their trains and aeroplanes and girls play with dolls and it keeps on so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will change over time?

Subject:	Er, definitely I mean you've seen it in other industries where more and more women have come in and in some places completely taken over. Yeah, I think the industry will change – it has to, to become more modern and becomes – it will be you know for the European convention and things that are – you know, a new constitution and things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that it is masculine will ever cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	Erm, I don't think so at all. I think as a female there are more advantages. You get noticed more than any male colleague even if you do have to maybe prove yourself a bit more.

Interviewer:	OK, you said earlier about having problems with having a family and that when you're in the RAF. Do you think that would be the same if you were in the engineering industry?

Subject:	No, not at all. I mean you can do what you want. I mean once you're 9 till 5 or you know 8.30 till 5.30 er it's over, it's completely your time, it's like the – normally you're not gonna work.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that there are any conflicts for women between choosing a career and a family, especially in such a sort of masculine environment?

Subject:	Oh I don't – I suppose some women erm sort of – feminist type women, wouldn't want to have a family because that maybe showed a weakness or something but to me, I'm quite comfortable with the whole – the whole thing, so..I don't think so, for me, anyway.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the people that you would be working with though, would find it an issue even if you didn't yourself?

Subject:	I don't know, I don't know what men think if you suddenly go and have a baby. Probably – slacker, because you'd get quite a lot of time off. But then again that's – you know you've got these new rules coming in now that men get paternity leave as well. So I think that's coming round a bit. Maybe, say 5 years ago, there would be – you know you probably would be very upset if you went off to have a baby for sort of 3 months out of work. I think it's getting better.

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything, thank you very much that was very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you doing aeronautical engineering then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And, are you going on a placement or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, the reason I ask is because we are mainly interviewing placement students but we do want to interview a few non-placement students to find out why they're not doing the placement. But the gist of the whole project is we're interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines to find out why they decided to do engineering, what they expect to get out of it, what their career ambitions are – things like that, but ultimately the people that are going on placement, we're going to go back and interview them again, when they're on placement, to find out whether it meets up to their expectations and the ultimate aim really is to make a practical guidance document for the Engineering Councils so hopefully it will improve the situation for women in engineering. I'll start by asking you a few background questions and then we can move on to ask about the course so far and what you want to do long-term.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What A levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did maths, physics and geology.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was just a normal high school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, it wasn't an all girls' school or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I used to work at a factory for aeroplane assembly, during my summer holidays and they restore Spitfire and Hurricane, sort of with 1950's techniques. Erm, like I said I do – I go there every time I (got/get?) a few weeks off to do a little bit more, but not in the mainstream industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, that sounds really interesting. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no but my dad's a technology teacher and he's – he's now a computer technician.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK then, when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it probably started when I was a child. I was one of these kids that always had Meccano or Lego and I just found that I had a knack for maths and physics, so I thought engineering would be great to do. Also, I wanted to be an engineer, as a career, that's what I wanted to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that anything else has influenced you, like your family or with your dad probably being involved in like technology, or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think it's very much my dad's influence. Er because he used to take me to model car racing and model air – you know – plane - flying things from a very early age.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK did you have much careers advice when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think I can remember one interview, where I just told them what I wanted to do and everything but not, not really. They've more taken an idea along that they'd tell you how to get where you wanted to be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what did they say about you wanting to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they said that was really good. Erm, and they said – I said aeronauticals and they said you know a few other engineering areas to look into.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much career research?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, I went through probably about 15 – like a keeping of a folder of everything that looked good and kept on checking things out till I decided what…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It sounds very organised.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was. I was a strange child.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it then, that appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, maybe it's just – it's really interesting. I look at everything and I want to know how it works. Erm, and with engineering, well they teach you how it works. Erm, basically – it's the jobs you can get with engineering are very exciting and – well, the majority are – and you've got the teams and other people with the same ideas, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's what appeals to you about doing aeronautical engineering, did you ever consider any other type of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I considered a few types but with aeronautical it's – I liked it because it was so broad, you learnt everything from you know, electrical to mechanical to you know say systems and programming. But then the case studies are all linked to aircraft which was where my main interest lay, in the end.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that sounds good. How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [This university] – I – well one of my teachers went to [this university] and he used to sing its praises, as an engineer. And I came here for 2 day erm engineering look around of all the departments – weekend can't remember what it was called – and I loved the campus. And when I actually came that was about 2 years before I came to university but when I actually went round all the open days it just turned out that [this university] – you know, it was the best and I'd had the best experience here as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you realise when you decided that you wanted to do engineering, that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I did yes but the thing is with the way I was brought up, going to like model shows and you know model flying, it was quite often I was the only girl in the building and at the thing. So it turned out – so most of my friends, at a younger age, were male anyway, so it didn't seem to ..

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged, or enabled, to take engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, very much so – definitely. I mean if they are interested in it, because you find that not many females are actually interested in engineering. I don't know whether it's how they're brought up or – actually they should be forced into it, but if they have a general interest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women aren't given the opportunity to have an interest, because they don't even know what engineering is in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah. Very much. I think it would be nice, if at younger age you could go into girls and say look, you can do it, it's not just for lads. Erm, …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and sort of raise awareness.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but it's very much – I think it's done from when I was at the age of 3 – I got my first set of Lego or something and my – I think when you're having – a girl having a very close interest, you know, or a woman that knows about engineering going in at a very early – you know, formative years.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh, erm, you've got to be able to think logically, that's quite key for engineering. Also, I've met quite a few engineers that don't have any people skills at all and engineers, with a good degree, is going to be a Manager, so I think very much understanding how people work and so learning a bit about management – it's all pretty much key to engineering as a graduate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would describe any of those things as more male or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know. Being general – almost sexist – I think females very much have the good people – good people skills but maybe I don't know, maybe not as logical in the way think – it's more emotional – I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do you think are the advantages or disadvantages of being a female engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's loads of – I think there's loads of advantages because as you are maybe the only female – one of 3 or 4 females in a room of engineers, erm you'll very much get noticed. And if you've got a viewpoint you'll find that people – you know, the men especially, will listen to you erm rather than maybe another sort of identical male. Erm, some disadvantages – I don't know, I've not come across that many disadvantages other than maybe with the older generation they see you – females – we have to work harder to prove, yes you are just as intelligent as the person sitting next to you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you ever felt like you have to work harder – is that just what you imagine it to be like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in some situations. If you're going into a group that's already formed it's quite hard to say, look actually I do have an idea and it's better than yours or you know, it might help it. But no, when I worked at (?) Assemblies, they were lovely old gentlemen and they erm you know once I actually started talking, I had actually shown an interest, they were very accepting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, this year it has. The first year I was getting a little bit disillusioned because it's all sorts of maths and all basics and there's no aircraft in it erm but yeah, this year's really good, actually learning how to design an aircraft from scratch.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the gender proportions – what are the gender proportions on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, there's 9 females out of 140 people on the course, I think. It's a bit low.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think that the best thing is that everyone's sort of gelled really well. When we did a end of term sort of 2 weeks after everyone else has gone home and building model aircrafts and all you know, just playing – that bit's really good fun. Erm the worst bit's – I think it's the thermodynamics – I went to a module and I passed it and everything but I just didn't understand what was going on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you get any help with that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we had – the lecturer was great on it – we just – we all just kind of missed the point.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Overall then, are you pleased that you did choose this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very pleased. I don't think I would have taken any other course – looking back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, that's really good. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er yes, [name] took us for dynamics and vibrations.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you noticed any differences in the style of teaching of the male and the female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I don't know I can only really base it on just on one lecturer, because originally we had another kind of female lecturer but it was for kind of business, and it was completely different module that we were taught anyway. I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't know if I'd find it more encouraging. It – probably it would be nice to see, you know, more women in you know – people that are in engineering but I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the female lecturer treats you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, she did. I mean she's got quite an interesting personality. She's – I don't know she's kind of funny in a very dry way, whereas some of the other lecturers are – I don't know – not funny at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about the male lecturers, do you think they treat the female students the same as the male students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, I think they do erm there's only been one case where we've kind of – he's more of a technician, but he kinds of pats you on head and sends you off but no, it's all been very fair,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes – male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with having a male tutor – do you find him approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he's a brilliant chap, he's really interesting – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You wouldn't prefer to have a female tutor then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't mind really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know really. Er, one of our – teaching lecturers, he's really nice and he's always interested in what you want to do and what you're going to do and sort of banters you back about – erm, 'cos I wanted to be a navigator – why is a navigator getting an engineering degree?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you had to do a lot of group work as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, quite a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I do in most situation's – I mean there's a – I like everybody normally, but there's one or two people on my course that I always get put in a group with and erm, I sit there and I just grit my teeth a little bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well why is that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, generally he's the best thing since sliced bread and everything he's – everything you've done he's done 10 times better. He doesn't really take in your viewpoint. But he does that with everybody, it's not just females.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think males are more likely to have that attitude than a female though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, ooh that's a hard one, erm, hmm, you know with – females that do engineering, definitely men will have more of that attitude but the ones I've met so far seem to be very level headed and nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you deal with that situation then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh it's – it's fine really. You just – I just sit there and nod and whenever we sort of carry on our discussions and – I mean he has some good ideas, you've just got to sort of filter them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the benefits of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it's (?) – especially with engineering if you're – we just designed a frame to take a certain loading, and there's so many areas that you've got to cover and sort of like – the analysis of stresses, and what sort of (routes?) you're gonna use, you very much need more brains. So each person can focus on a different bit. And if you're focusing on something different, it's always good to get them to look at your bit and you look at their bit, because you very much get caught up in one area and forget about another area because of – well it's just so broad – you've got to learn everything – loads of things about this one item you're making.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will help you when you go into the industry – the fact that you've done so much group work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, I think they do. I mean I've worked within teams which I've been the only female in, and I've worked in teams which have – you know – are usually (?) male or female. Erm, I think with erm – with a male group it's normally quite raucous, by itself, but a female group brings a – sort of a very civilising influence into it. I remember from being a child that there'd be you know, basically the cars and then all these chaps would normally be mouthing off, and then you'd put a sort of 12 year old girl in the situation, and you've never met such polite like people, in the world, hopefully. But yes, stabilising influence.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you've said you've worked with male groups and female groups. Do you have a preference or aren't you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm not really bothered. I mean – because the people – anybody you're working with in a group is so different, you couldn't really compare them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I did yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide not to do the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I'm doing the 4 years masters – er and I kind of thought maybe 5 years is too long. Erm, I mean if I could – I could have done a 3 year and had a year in industry and realised that's good to employers because I'd done the year in industry and had experience but then I thought well if I do the – I want – I'm gonna – touch wood – I'll end up doing the masters and maybe in a few years time become chartered (yeah). And if – you know if I've got to do this masters anyway, I might as well do it all in a row, while your brains in the right gear than do a placement year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I was actually – I joined the RAF as a volunteer reserve

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh yeah, I think you said that in your email (sorry about that) That's OK.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And they're not really into – well they are this year but when I joined they weren't really into people doing gap years because you have to leave your squadron, and then sort of re-apply (absolutely) and I didn't really want to lose you know, the opportunities that I had. Erm, but this year they actually do – they are including a placement year, we sussed it about 2 months ago, so I probably could've done that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any particular advantages, or disadvantages of doing the gap year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, disadvantages, as I've said to you – maybe a year out of the flow of all of your course. That if you get more money – so you can afford to stay for that extra year, but the advantages are very much – well one of my friends has done a 3 year straight – erm mechanical engineering course and she's going on to get a job in the industry and the first sort of 5 places she applied to said, oh we're just using people with a year's experience. Erm, because again there's so many people now with erm a Bachelor's course and their experiences – they can – you know they can pick and choose their graduate training schemes. So I think if I was just doing a Bachelor's I'd be a bit worried about not doing a placement year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact that you're doing a masters counteracts that a bit then, when you will be looking for a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so, yes. That's the plan.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the work experience that you've done and the fact that you are a RAF volunteer, do you think that'll help when you're looking for a job as well – that experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, that's another thing that I'm hoping because I've had so much management and leadership training and you know they've taken me all around the world, so I such be a bold enough person without the gap year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How long have you been an RAF volunteer for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was a year last December – it seems much longer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sorts of things does that involve then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, oh every Tuesday we have a training night er and we learn all about current affairs er what the RAF is, the aircraft coming in. Every free day I go to RAF [place] and I'm learning to fly erm on the – an air flight training scheme, which when I complete, I'll be streamed and then I can go on from there if I decide to join the RAF as a pilot or a navigator. Erm, you get adventure training, which is practically free. I mean I went to Egypt for 10 days for £110 and we did a 15 hour diving course

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That sounds exciting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And also, I've been to Tanzania for 5 weeks, built an orphanage with an RAF team and then went on safari with (?) (wow) – brilliant. But you have 2 years kind of completely free and then you have to apply – I've just applied to the RAF for – for the 4 day Officer's selection board and I'm just awaiting the results to see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that for when you've finished Uni or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it'll be a bursary scheme, so I wouldn't be allowed to do a gap year anyway, if I get the bursary.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so they'll sponsor you for like your last…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. So I went for my pilot in engineering because I have really enjoyed the flying and I thought well if you never have – if you never apply, you never try and I don't know you'll never know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I had flying lessons for my 18th birthday. What do you think have been the best things and the worst things about the RAF experience and the other work experience that you've had?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I can't think of any bad things. Erm, it was good. Well the only thing I can say is when you're in the RAF, everything that you do is assessed, every time you talk to one of the staff they make a mental note and it all comes down to a final year report, but my report's all been good, so touch wood I've achieved what they want – you know what they think's good enough.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you worked with many women while you've been in the RAF?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think – er not really erm other than people that are sort of my age, erm or in the non-commissioned ranks there's a lot of females but in the sort of pilot course I've mainly been taught by pilots and there didn't seem to be hardly any female pilots. I only know of er – I know 1 navigator and 1 pilot that are actually just starting their first tours.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the main skills that you'll learn from both the work experiences, that you'll take into industry with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, with doing work on – in 1950's – you kind of learn a bit of history of flight and you've always got – if you're talking to another engineer there'll always be – or anybody really, they will always be interested about that, so there's always something you know, or what sort of (?) you can tell them about this. So, just kind of a general interest, you can get that from it.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, with the RAF it takes all leadership erm and you learn so much about people because you're put in very stressful situations and told right, can you get these people to you know do this. And you panic for a bit but then you suddenly realise that actually everyone's – if everyone knows you really, you can tell them what to do, and they do it, and they help you with suggestions and in the end you become – you know, you do become part of a team.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the whole educational experience and the way you're taught, reflects what it's like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't know. I don't think - industry – I have this idea of industry that it'll be sort of all kind of suits and big Board meetings and things like that. Whereas going to university in your jeans and baggy T-shirts kind of thing and sitting in front of a Board. I think where my course is very lecture based, and because of funding it's not very hands on and the team work is kind of more informal. Erm, I don't think it's exactly what industry will be like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think it should be geared more to prepare you for when you go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way, yes. I mean systems is very geared up. I mean they have come into university, in suits, every now and then to do their big Board meetings and things. But, from a student's point of view you kind of don't want that hassle if you see what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you hope to work for the RAF when you finish your degree then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it is. I'd love to. I mean on the Squadron, I'm a navigator, but unfortunately they're not taking any more on, they've got too many at the moment so unless I – if I don't get this bursary I'll go in direct entrants and apply navigator first, then engineer. Erm, but I think the – well, I hope the outcome from this – I've just applied for – erm will – either be a pilot bursary, which I'd be over the moon with. Erm, but I think more likely I'll be an engineer but er that's what I hope to – if I accept the bursary I'll have to do 16 years, but that's what I want really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Fantastic. How do you think that work will differ from being at university, in terms of what's expected of you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in the RAF it'll be completely different. Erm, I've followed around the Engineering Officer for a day when I was on a flight station and you're taught – you're taught a very broad course, here at university but the stuff he was doing was completely different again because he had erm he was a junior engineering officer and he'd got 5 aircraft, he was responsible for keeping up and running all the time. He's got 160 non-commissioned officers that he was in charge of and he was – I think he was 5 years older than I am. Erm, that's the level of responsibility. He spent quite a lot of time sifting paperwork, another lot of time in high level meetings trying to convince his senior officers that yes, they will have their aircraft and no this one is very broken – you're not having it. It's all people skills. He only once or twice had to use his engineering background to say you know, no, this is – it's not fit to fly. But the degree is there for when you sign your name on a bit of paper and if – you know – the worst happens, it's mainly for what's your job title in court type of thing. See what I mean? It's more of a compulsory requirement, to be an engineering officer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you mind that or would you prefer it if you were actually using more of your degree or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, a good – no, I think I would really enjoy the people management. But as you progress up the ladder you need to use your engineering degree more erm because you'll be looking at bringing new technologies, which is eventually what I'd like to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you still get your chartership if you go to work in the RAF?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, you do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the main skills that you will use from the degree, when you are working? Do you think it will then be more like relationship skills rather than the actual technical skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, I think it will be erm I've done a few business modules and I think that will come in – they will be important. But from the degree, it's compulsory to be an engineer that you have a – you know, a technical background so I will use it as in I have to have it and I just find it really interesting anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think the best and the worst things about working in the RAF?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the best things are it's not just a career its a lifestyle – you've got – you know, you have to see – they own you for 12 hours a day and if they want to fill those 12 hours then they get filled. Erm but the opportunities are unbelievable. I mean I've only been in a year and I've you know, seen so much erm there's – I think the benefits of joining the RAF far outweigh, you know the disadvantages, 'cos obviously you are a member of a fighting force and if it comes to war you're going to war – that's what they pay you for. Erm, but you know it's just…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that the only disadvantage that you could say?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, there's also one – if I'm a pilot I won't be able to have children till I've you know, done quite a lot of service, because obviously they've spent quite a few million pounds training you – they don't want you to suddenly get pregnant and run off.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really because my mum had me when she was I think she was 30 – my brother when she was 34 and by the time I've done my 16 years or done say 14 years and then doing ground tour I'll be about that age anyway, so, you know, touch wood I'll be able to have kids.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there's anything that will stop you from achieving what you want in terms of your career? Or any difficulties that you might face?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't think so – apart from failing my degree, that would just stop everything in its tracks, but I can't really see that. Other than, you know, the worst happening at home and having to go back in…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far or would you do anything differently if you had to go through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm happy so far. I'll – you know, I'll let you know in a few weeks if I'm very happy or if I'm going back to the drawing board.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you considered any other options if you don't get into the RAF?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, er I – 1 applied 2 years ago and er I was a little bit too young. You know they said grow up a little bit come back. And I applied for [company] undergraduate scheme, as well – sort of joint venture between [company] and can't remember – some other, other companies and they actually said, yes, we'll give you sponsorship. But by the time they'd given me a letter of confirmation, I'd joined the er Squadron and I'd got you know 10 weeks of adventure training. I just couldn't pass it up to do 10 weeks of work placement. So I rejected that but they – I think very much I wouldn't have a problem getting back into that sort of area so er yeah I'll work for the highest bidder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things would you be looking for in a company if you don't go in the RAF? What sort of things would attract you to a company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very much good promotional prospects – er it'd have to be a big successful company er because they're the only ones that have good promotional prospects. Basically I wanted – I want a very strong company because quite a few little ones have been going under recently because of – you've got all the problem of the aircraft industry – they're moving it all abroad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That's probably the hardest question you could ask an engineers. Erm, challenging, fun, interesting, corporation, integral.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know. I suppose you would because it is mainly full of men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is what makes it masculine – the numbers of men rather than the type of work that you're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would say yes, I think, because erm I don't know if it was full of women you'd say it was feminine because obviously the industry takes on the character of the people that are in it. Erm, I don't know – traditionally it's very masculine because you know boys play with their trains and aeroplanes and girls play with dolls and it keeps on so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will change over time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, definitely I mean you've seen it in other industries where more and more women have come in and in some places completely taken over. Yeah, I think the industry will change – it has to, to become more modern and becomes – it will be you know for the European convention and things that are – you know, a new constitution and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact that it is masculine will ever cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't think so at all. I think as a female there are more advantages. You get noticed more than any male colleague even if you do have to maybe prove yourself a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you said earlier about having problems with having a family and that when you're in the RAF. Do you think that would be the same if you were in the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all. I mean you can do what you want. I mean once you're 9 till 5 or you know 8.30 till 5.30 er it's over, it's completely your time, it's like the – normally you're not gonna work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that there are any conflicts for women between choosing a career and a family, especially in such a sort of masculine environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I don't – I suppose some women erm sort of – feminist type women, wouldn't want to have a family because that maybe showed a weakness or something but to me, I'm quite comfortable with the whole – the whole thing, so..I don't think so, for me, anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the people that you would be working with though, would find it an issue even if you didn't yourself?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know, I don't know what men think if you suddenly go and have a baby. Probably – slacker, because you'd get quite a lot of time off. But then again that's – you know you've got these new rules coming in now that men get paternity leave as well. So I think that's coming round a bit. Maybe, say 5 years ago, there would be – you know you probably would be very upset if you went off to have a baby for sort of 3 months out of work. I think it's getting better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's everything, thank you very much that was very helpful.
